title: Delight
hookLine: Isaiah calls Shabbat a delight; enjoyment itself is part of it
tomorrow: is a Saturday nap lazy, or holy? one verb in Exodus decides.

cards: Plenty of people treat enjoyment like a reward you earn after the list is done: finish everything, then you're allowed one good thing, and by then you're usually too tired to enjoy it.
Isaiah has one word for how Shabbat should feel, and it isn't duty, and it isn't even rest. It's delight. Here's the verse, and then the whole week comes back for one round.

teach.b: Isaiah says, in the old Jewish translation: "And call the sabbath a delight."
The Hebrew word is oneg. Not endurance. Pleasure.
The Talmud takes it literally and asks: with what do you delight in it?

teach.h: BEETS, FISH, GARLIC, OR SOMETHING SMALL.
teach.b: One sage answers with a menu: a dish of beets, a big fish, heads of garlic. Another says even a small thing, if it's made in honor of Shabbat, counts as delight. Notice the condition: made in honor of Shabbat.
The beets aren't special on their own. Setting them aside for this day is what turns a vegetable into a delight.
So oneg isn't an extra on top of the real Shabbat. It's one of the ways Shabbat is kept. Now look back at the week with that word.

The song at the table was oneg. The empty hands without a phone made room for it. The slow walk, the candle for one, the dessert a child waits for, the friend who came and only had to eat: oneg, every one.
Which is the thing to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, a plate of beets can be a way of keeping a commandment.
Delight isn't the prize at the end. It's the point.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat make room for oneg, delight: good food saved for the day, songs, rest, time with family and friends, and reading; the custom is that enjoyment itself honors the day.

o: the blessing said when Shabbat comes to an end
delight: enjoying Shabbat as part of keeping it
a sweet dessert eaten only on Friday nights

games.q: a week of delight — tap the pairs.

s: Isaiah calls the Sabbath a delight
Isaiah 58:13: "And call the sabbath a delight."
enjoying Shabbat too much takes away from its holiness
the Talmud asks how to delight in it, and answers with food.
delight on Shabbat has to be something lavish
even a small thing made in its honor counts, says the Talmud.

games.q: your aunt feels guilty eating cake on Saturday afternoon when she "should be doing something religious." what does Isaiah's word say?
o: the cake can be the religious part: Isaiah calls Shabbat a delight.
she should save treats for after Shabbat ends tonight.
it depends on whether she's said enough prayers first.
games.why: oneg is one of the ways Shabbat is kept. the Talmud's own examples of delight are food.

practice: Count on your fingers five small delights from this past week, the kind that usually get skipped: a good cup of something, a song in the car, a laugh, a cool sheet at night.
For each finger, pause long enough to taste it again before moving on.

wordCard.voice: Oneg: delight. Isaiah's word for how Shabbat should feel, from a plate of beets to a hum at the table.

orig.note: Hebrew: delight, pleasure. Isaiah 58:13 calls the Sabbath oneg.

carryVoice: Your line: delight is the point. Not the reward at the end; the thing itself. That's a week, enjoyed.

sources.q: And call the sabbath a delight
